speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to move, seconded by Mr. MacEachen, that this house do now adjourn. I move this motion, in accordance with an agreement among the parties in the house, so it may initiate a discussion of housing and urban development between this hour and, I believe, one o'clock. I have the privilege of introducing this subject, and I hope to set a good example by giving a very brief statement. Before the discussion is concluded, I hope the minister responsible for housing may be able to wind it up and deal with points which may be raised.
Why isn't he leading oft?

Because I am leading off, which may not be a very adequate reason but is the best I can think of at the moment.
As the house knows, a federal-provincial housing conference was held in Ottawa a short time ago. I had the honour to preside over it, although I was not able to attend all the sessions. It has been described as having been a failure; because it collapsed prematurely and some of the premiers walked out of the conference before it ended. I should point out that the letters to the premiers invited them to come to Ottawa to discuss this subject and to exchange views on this very important and urgent problem at a meeting beginning on Monday, December 11 and continuing perhaps for another day or two.
In my opening statement I expressed the hope that we might be able to complete the discussions by Tuesday night, but that if not we would go on until Wednesday. We did, in fact finish our work before the third day, and the premiers who were here at the beginning were here at the end. Indeed, I recall very well a dinner which was held on Tuesday night, a very useful and friendly dinner at which all the premiers who were here at the conference were present.
So it was not a question of the conference breaking up. Before it completed its discussion, arrangements had been made and agreed on for the federal and provincial deputy ministers responsible for housing in their particular governments to meet in three , months to follow up some of the subjects that were raised at this conference, and for the ministers responsible for housing in the various governments to meet together in six months.
The purpose of the conference, as indicated in the invitation, was to examine the very important and serious problem of housing and urban development and to see what could be done co-operatively-because that is the only way in which progress can be made -to improve the situation.
As all spokesmen at the conference pointed out at one time or another, the problem is basically one of urbanization in our country. The process of urbanization in Canada has now reached the point where the concentration of population in urban centres is proceeding apace. At the present time 75 per cent of our people live in cities or towns. I am informed that by 1980, at the present rate of progress, two thirds of the people of Canada will live in 29 urban centres and one third will live in three metropolitan centres.
Housing is only one, but certainly the most immediate and urgent, of the problems rising out of urbanization and urban development. As all hon. members know, the problem is to keep pace with this development in terms of the number of houses required for adequate or better than adequate housing, and to improve the quality as well as the quantity of our housing. Progress has been made in this field. I may have a few figures to give, though the minister will have a chance to go into the subject in greater detail. There has been progress in recent years, of course, but that progress is not sufficient. Perhaps the most impressive indication of the problem, what has been done and what is required to be done, which is more than has been done, is contained in the fourth report of the Economic Council of Canada. This report was often quoted during the discussions.

December 21, 1967
Housing
[DOT] (10:10 a.m.)
There are, of course, related problems in urbanization in addition to housing. I will only mention problems such as transportation and pollution. There is also the matter of cost, which has something to do with the whole problem. The fact is that as we all know the cost of housing has gone up 50 per cent in 15 years, in spite of the efficiency of the housing industry. The efficiency of this industry has been increasing, in part at least due to the assistance given and investigations carried out by governments, including the federal government. But while costs have gone up 50 per cent in 15 years it is only right to point out, on the other hand, that incomes have gone up by 100 per cent.
Perhaps the most difficult, the most serious factor in connection with increased costs is the cost of land, both raw land and serviced land. This is a matter of more immediate importance, because it comes under their sole responsibility, to the municipal and provincial governments, although the federal government certainly has a relationship to the problem. One of the difficulties in dealing adequately with the housing problem, a difficulty which was faced at this conference, arises out of the complexity of the government closest to that problem, that is, municipal government. There are 18 cities in Canada now with populations of over 100,000 people, but there are 260 municipal jurisdictions covering those people. This of course makes it much more difficult than it would be otherwise to deal with the problems involved in housing and urban development, urban transportation, pollution and that kind of thing.
Now, Mr. Speaker, of course the immediate question is how best to deal with the problem. More money from Ottawa alone, important though that may be, is not the answer. During the last ten years the federal government has invested in privately initiated housing $3.5 billion. No doubt in future the government will have to invest more as opportunities and resources are available. But that alone is not the answer-that is, federal participation-for the simple reason that the provinces have the primary responsibility in this matter, not the sole but the primary responsibility.
This brings up the question, which is sometimes overlooked, the question of jurisdiction. It was made quite clear to us at the conference, by some provinces particularly,

that this whole matter was primarily a provincial one, and that the federal government should be very careful in intervening beyond its jurisdiction in this field. There was no doubt as to where certain provinces stood in that regard. I know there are those who feel that to the greatest extent possible we should go ahead ignoring constitutional difficulties; full speed ahead and damn the constitutional torpedoes.
Hear, hear.

I hear "Hear, hear" from the other side. If we went full speed ahead in this country of ours and said damn the constitutional torpedoes, we would not keep the ship afloat for very long. While this, of course, is of fundamental importance, there is no question, Mr. Speaker, about federal responsibility. This is a national problem as well as a provincial problem. If it were not a national problem the federal government would not have invested those sums I have mentioned in the last 10 or 15 years. But we have attended to our responsibilities in this, and in similar fields, with full regard to the jurisdictional and constitutional rights and responsibilities of the provinces.
We had a discussion on pollution at this conference. If anything could be national in scope and in impact, surely it is pollution. The air does not stop at any provincial border, nor do rivers stop at a provincial border. We were warned, however, in connection with pollution matters that we should be very careful about interfering with provincial action in this field. We do not want to interfere, we want to assist. While the initiation in respect of these matters in many cases must come from the provinces we must help them and work with them within their jurisdiction as is laid down in the constitution.
We have helped. We have taken steps which we expect will improve the mortgage market and get more private money into housing. I am not going to go into those steps because they are well known. There were differences of opinion at the conference about the effectiveness of these measures, whether we had in fact increased the amount of money coming into the market. Perhaps the Minister of Labour will be able to deal with that. However, one thing has been shown. If we had not taken these measures while perhaps they have not increased the amount of money to the extent we would have liked, there would have been very little, if any, mortgage money coming into the market at
December 21, 1967

this time. The results, therefore, while not perhaps as encouraging as we would have hoped, have certainly shown an improvement.
At the very beginning of the conference, and not as a result of provincial pressures as has been sometimes indicated nor in accordance with provincial proposals as has been suggested, the federal government made four concrete proposals which are of great importance and which would enlarge the activities of the federal government in this field. I do not believe sufficient attention has been given to these proposals or the effect they could have on housing in this country if they are taken up by the provinces. I admit that we could probably operate with the provinces to a greater extent in putting them into effect in years to come than we can this year because of financial difficulties; nevertheless even this year there will be more money available for this kind of federal assistance than there was last year.
Now 1 want to put these proposals, which improve and enlarge the lending procedures, on the record because they are important. They were outlined to the conference in my opening statement and subsequently in the background paper which was circulated. The first proposal provides for federal-provincial participation in comprehensive planning of our urban regions in advance; the acquisition of land for transportation corridors and open spaces for recreation and similar community purposes. This is a new initiative on the part of the federal government for federal action, as are the others I am going to mention.
The second is federal-provincial support for land assembly and development of comprehensively planned new suburban communities within urban areas. This is a very important proposal which in some countries has had very important results, and I am thinking now particularly of Great Britain.
The third proposal is for housing subsidy programs to serve as an integral part of other combined federal-provincial anti-poverty measures in special areas characterized by general poverty, lack of employment opportunities and slow economic growth. This would provide for selling as well as renting housing at below cost in those areas.
The fourth proposal is for a more vigorously supported program to assist growing families to locate homes, many of whom require not small apartments but three or four bedroom accommodation and good community
Housing
facilities within reach of their moderate incomes.
These are important proposals. As I say, they will require amendment to our legislation and we will be bringing in those amendments as soon as possible. They will also require full co-operation from the provinces so we can work together in these new fields of federal-provincial action. They will require, in due course, massive amounts of money, provincially, municipally and federally. Suggestions have been made, Mr. Speaker, that we will have no money next year, or less money than last year for this special purpose, but that is not the ease.
[DOT] (10:20 a.m.)
Before I conclude, Mr. Speaker, perhaps I should say a word about the 1967 housing record, and then say something about the proposal we made for a council to be set up in the field of housing.
The record in 1967 is not good enough to deal with the problems that we face, problems which have been exposed to us by, among others, the economic council. To meet these problems satisfactorily we will require 175,000 or 180,000 starts a year. This year housing starts throughout Canada should reach about 160,000, which is 26,000 units better than last year and approaches the highest figure that has ever been reached.
To the end of November of this year total National Housing Act participation in new housing involved approximately $921 million. Of this amount more than $610 million represented direct government loans for residential construction. It is that kind of assistance, especially in regard to certain kinds of public housing, for poor or underprivileged people, the provision of student residences and things of that kind, that will be available next year, I hope in equal if not larger amounts; and this notwithstanding our financial difficulties. We expect more money from the private sector to go into private housing, and this will leave more government money available for public housing.
We also proposed at the conference the establishment on a federal provincial basis -though we did indicate that we would be willing to pay for the establishment and maintenance of the machinery-of a council on housing and urban development, a proposal which did not get immediate acceptance on the part of the provinces. I was a little surprised at that, because I think this can be a very important development.

December 21, 1967
Housing
The case for such a council has been put very effectively, more effectively than I can put it, by a body that is continually being quoted in this and other fields, namely the Economic Council of Canada, which is now an economic body outside government that is investigating and doing research to advise government. I think no one now claims that this is a useless piece of machinery that is getting in the way of the federal government, though there are times when the federal government does think its advice is perhaps not the most constructive in the world from the point of view of our responsibilities. This is bound to occur with an independent body, but its very independence is its value.
Is there no place, Mr. Speaker, for this kind of research and investigation through a federal-provincial council in this other important field? The fourth report of the Economic Council of Canada has this to say at page 268 on the subject of housing and urban development:
The essential need is for a synthesis, a comprehensive philosophy, a co-ordinated concept of urban development. This applies both to the largest metropolitan areas, where expansion and decentralization need to be framed within the setting of the broad urban region, and to the city complexes of more modest size where rates and problems of growth will nevertheless still be formidable.
The report continues:
-in no area of government affairs are there more glaring gaps and deficiencies of data, information and understanding than in urban problems and government. This is not to deny the many useful efforts to improve the situation. But there is an immense need for more and better co-ordinated study and research in this field.
It was in an effort to meet this need on a federal-provincial and not merely a federal basis that we put forward what I believe to have been a useful and constructive proposal, one which was undoubtedly considered as such by the economic council when they wrote this report. That is the basis behind our proposal for a Canadian council on housing and urban development to be established jointly.
There is no thought in this proposal, Mr. Speaker, of establishing merely another committee of government officials, federal, provincial and municipal, to create some new bureaucracy to produce new but inactive uses for old papers and reports to meet the problems in this field. This was not the purpose, and it was made clear that it need not be the result of the acceptance of a proposal of this kind. A council of this kind would in

a sense have the same relationship to government in the field of housing and urban development as the economic council. It would consist of outside experts in this field. No council of this kind is now doing the job on a national basis.
The purpose, then, was to establish-and I hope this purpose will still be realized-an impartial and influential body that could act as a kind of public conscience, a spur for urban development in Canada, encouraging government at every level to do the necessary things in this field. It could publish reports, it could publish reviews on a regional and a national basis, and it could offer specific suggestions to all governments on priorities and solutions for both the immediate and the long term problems. This kind of reporting and investigation could serve as the basis for the annual meetings which I believe will take place between provincial ministers and a federal minister dealing with housing problems.
This was not an excuse for inaction, Mr. Speaker. This was a proposal to make possible more action, more intelligent, planned action on a national basis so as to help not only the federal government but each provincial government in the field of housing. There is no comparable body in the national field. As I say, I think this was a very useful proposal, and when the provincial governments give it further consideration they may also decide the proposal is a useful one. However, it is up to them; if they do not wish to participate that is their responsibility, and no doubt they will continue to operate through their own provincial bodies in this field.
I have ventured, Mr. Speaker, to indicate some of the problems in the field of housing as well as some of the results from the exchange of views at this conference. In particular there were the four proposals which were put forward and which could lead to very far reaching federal and provincial developments in the field of housing; that indeed could lead, if the provinces so desired and within their own constitutional jurisdiction, to an even greater participation than that which has taken place in earlier years by the federal government in a field of very great and serious importance, one that is likely to become even more so.

Mr. Speaker, we have three hours only to debate this very important matter of housing and urban development. I intended to keep
December 21, 1967

my speech to the minimum time and to appeal to all members of the house to cut down their speeches, because on our side alone there are seven members who are very anxious to speak. Of this valuable time the Prime Minister has taken something like 20 or 25 minutes, and I am wondering whether we are any better off now having heard his speech.
One result of his speech, Mr. Speaker, is that I will have to spend a little more time than I had intended in order to correct some of the impressions the right hon. gentleman left. For example, the Prime Minister seemed to be quite happy or proud about the fact that this year there will be 160,000 starts, which he said was some 26 per cent more than last year. But what he does not say, Mr. Speaker, is that the number of starts last year was 134,000, which is less than the number of starts in 1955, 12 years ago. Furthermore, the number of starts this year, 160,000, is 4,000 fewer than in 1965. As a matter of fact it is 4,000 starts fewer than in 1958. But apparently the government and the Prime Minister are quite happy with the fact that there was a big increase over the miserable year of 1966.
[DOT] (10:30 a.m.)
I agree with the Prime Minister that we cannot rely entirely on government money to finance housing. I agree also that government money primarily is required to provide housing for those people in need. But what the Prime Minister has overlooked is that although it is not essential that government money alone finance housing, it is essential that the fiscal business of the country be so arranged that private money at a reasonable interest rate is available to finance housing. That is the crux of the problem that faces us today. I recognize that the government has put over $900 million into housing this year, but that was necessary because of the mismanagement of the fiscal affairs of this country which has meant that private money at a reasonable interest rate has not been available to those who need housing.
The suggestion of the Prime Minister at the conference, that a council be established to deal with this problem, has a great deal of merit; but I submit that because of the attitude of the government in respect of the growth of bureaucracy there is suspicion in the minds of the people and the provincial governments that any suggestion of the federal government in this direction is made just to enlarge the growth of bureaucracy. I
Housing
think this is one reason the provinces immediately rejected the idea of such a council. I hope when a government that does not encourage the growth of bureaucracy comes into office the provinces will recognize that this is not just a growth of bureaucracy but might be of benefit in solving this problem, even though the suggestion be implemented in some modified form.
Many times in the past year we have discussed the matter of housing. On October 2 when we were debating a supply motion I made a motion which read in part as follows:
And this house regrets the failure of the government to recognize the housing shortage as a major crisis requiring immediate and co-ordinated steps for its solution as clearly indicated by the recent report of the Economic Council of Canada.
We had a two day debate on this subject at that time. We also had debates on the matter earlier this year. What has happened since that time? The situation is worse; there has been no improvement. Perhaps I should qualify that and say the only improvement has been a slight increase in housing starts, but the cost of housing has been so high that the average Canadian has been unable to avail himself of the facilities of the money market.
Prices have increased since that time. The Toronto Daily Star of December 13 published an article which quoted the president of the Toronto real estate board as saying that the price of a metro home will go up between 5 per cent and 10 per cent next year "because fumbling governments"-I do not say this government alone is responsible for the mess we are in with regard to housing, but it must bear the major part of the blame-"can't get together on the housing crisis." The president of the Toronto real estate board made many good suggestions in this article. I will not take the time to read them all, but would refer the minister to the article.
The president of the real estate board suggested the elimination of the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials used in new homes and in alterations to existing homes. That suggestion has been made over and over again. In spite of the shortage of housing and the increased cost the government persists in contributing materially to the increase in cost by maintaining the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. An article which appeared in the Vancouver Sun of December 13 said:
Meanwhile, there is no logical excuse for governments, supposedly striving to stimulate home construction, to deter it by taxation.

December 21, 1967'
Housing
This article then refers to the very interesting suggestion by Premier Johnson of Quebec that if the federal government would drop the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials he would remove the 8 per cent sales tax in that province. It is estimated that if this were done the cost of a $15,000 home in Quebec would be reduced by $1,300. This is an approach that could perhaps be used with the other provinces.
What else has happened since October 2? The cost of living has gone up. The war on poverty, which I assume would include those too poor to provide adequate housing for their families, has been abandoned. Taxation has been increased; the average Canadian will be paying more taxes starting January 1 next year, which will make him less able to buy a home. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour have confirmed that next year there will be even less government money available for housing. Because of the increase in the interest rate there may well be an increase in the private money available, but the cost will be so high the average Canadian will be even less able to finance a home for himself and his family. As a matter of fact the indications are that in spite of the proposed cuts in next year's budget the average Canadian will find that a house will be even more expensive. Hon. members will recall that in the speech from the throne there was reference to a federal-provincial conference on housing and urbanization. We urged the government to call this conference. The government did not heed our urging at that time, but we pinned our hopes on something concrete coming out of such a conference. I say to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Labour that in my opinion some of the suggestions made at the conference have a great deal of merit. Some of them are forward looking and in time will be of great help in solving this problem. I admit that.
I do not know how these federal-provincial conferences work. I do not know to what extent there is prior consultation. If I were a representative of a province and such proposals were thrown at me, I could not at that moment give any indication of the position I would take. I would want time to study the proposals. I know the Prime Minister has said there will be a conference of deputy ministers three months from now and of ministers six months from now, but I suggest that a conference of this type would be more fruitful if the provinces had advance notice of the proposals it was intended to put forward. I believe this is one reason the

federal-provincial conference did not bring: forth any valuable solutions to this problem.
The Prime Minister said the conference was not a complete flop. I do not know what has come out of it that is of value in the present situation. I should like to quote what other people have said about the conference. The Ottawa Journal of December 13 said:
Not a single additional house will he built in Canada as a dividend from the federal-provincial housing conference which broke up yesterday, a day early.
We find these words in the Hamilton Spectator of December 14:
The best comment on the federal-provincial housing conference is the silent one given by the delegates themselves: They did not wait for the end but departed one day early. The affair was a washout.
I recognize that the Prime Minister said there was a possibility it would last only two days, but this is what editorials in newspapers across the country are saying. The Charlottetown Guardian of December 14 said this:
The federal-provincial housing conference has petered out, leaving the housing crisis pretty much as it was, and the country still looking vainly for leadership from Ottawa.
The London Free Press, an important newspaper to certain parties, said in an editorial in its December 14 issue:
It can hardly be said that the latest federal-provincial conference contributed anything substantial toward the solution or amelioration of Canada's housing crisis.
I said when I began these remarks that I intended to keep my speech short so that other hon. members would have an opportunity to make their contributions. Many suggestions have been made to solve this problem. The fourth annual of the Economic Council of Canada contains a most important suggestion, namely that housing must be given a certain priority and the importance of housing to Canada must be recognized. I suspect that this government has not given due recognition to the importance of housing. It has not sufficiently recognized that this is a social matter of great importance to the Canadian people.
[DOT] (10:40 a.m.)
I will not take up the time of the house to say much more, but in a recent issue of a publication which is put out by the Canadian home builders association a number of suggestions are made which if adopted would assist in easing the housing problem. It
December 21, 1967

appears that such suggestions, and others which are made from time to time, fall on deaf ears. It seems that this government is incapable of solving the problem.
This government has lost the confidence of the people. It does not convey the impression that it is capable of solving the problems of Canada; and housing is merely one of this country's problems.
In case the Prime Minister has any doubt about the purport of my remarks, I say that it is essential for the government to comply with requests to make money available for housing. Certainly there are problems in planning, and the Prime Minister has not emphasized them enough, but money for houses must be made available. It need not necessarily be government money. The business of the country must be conducted in such a way that money at reasonable rates of interest is made available to fulfil the important needs of housing.

Mr. Speaker, may I say how pleased I am to see the Prime Minister here during this debate. At the conference, about which I shall say a word or two, his concern with the problem of housing was very, very evident. I am not convinced that the conference was a failure. Though not too much came of it, those of us who sat through it began to realize, if we did not realize it before, that in the area of housing we face a problem of nation-wide and staggering proportions. If there was any doubt about that before the conference, there was none afterward.
The conference also showed us how tremendously difficult it is to govern this country. The provinces, I think, came there and in effect told us "Give us money, and that is all we want." But the matter is not that simple. All the briefs that were filed and all the statements that were made emphasized the fantastic proportions of the housing crisis. They also emphasized our tremendous regional problems and the regional solutions that will be required.
It is purposeless in a debate like this to put on the record the dreary statistics showing how we failed in housing. I do not want to become partisan. I think we all realize that in the entire area of housing our people, all our governments have failed. Not only has the federal government failed; the provincial and municipal governments have also failed. So in this country we must somehow find 12 million houses before the end. of the century just to pick up the slack. How we are to get
Housing
those houses and how we are to finance them is the question we must ask ourselves.
It is a platitude to say there is no problem. This is a nation-wide problem; it is the most outstanding social problem that we face and as great as national defence. Our housing problem is about as great as any problem today. It is as great a problem as education, we can speak of.
I was glad to hear the Prime Minister say to the conference that the federal government has a wide area of responsibility in this matter. I realize the constitutional difficulties that he and his government face. My impression of the conference was not that those difficulties really created a barrier; instead, I thought the provinces were so desperate that they would welcome strong federal initiative and leadership in this area. The main impression I got from the conference was that the provinces, through their statements, admitted that they are incapable of solving the problem and that they are all desperately seeking a federal initiative in this entire area. There is no other way out of our difficulties. If the federal government will not assume some wide area of responsibility we shall never solve the housing crisis, and future generations will curse us for it.
Taking that initiative is not torpedoing the constitution-and I regret the phrase which had to be used. The provinces are looking for co-operation. No level of government alone can solve the housing problem; it can only be solved by a gigantic partnership of the federal government, provincial governments and municipalities. If we do not do this there is no hope at all.
At the conference I regretted to hear the minister conduct a whining, two day defence of a non-existent housing policy; because that is what we have in Ottawa and that is what we have had in Ottawa for the past 15 years under all governments. There has been no housing policy.
In this short debate we cannot detail a solution to the problem. That is impossible. The housing crisis has been with us much too long and it is much too deeply rooted for us, in a three hour debate, to begin to solve it. If the debate achieves nothing else it will have been worth while if we are able to establish that a crisis exists and that the federal government should assume a large degree of responsibility and leadership for a housing

December 21, 1967
Housing
program. This has never been done in Ottawa, and that has been my complaint since I arrived in the chamber.
Housing has always been treated as a pump primer. The government's policy has been that when employment goes down, it will throw a lot of mortgage money into the market. That creates tremendous dislocations in the building industry. There has never been any sustained flow of funds with which those who are interested in this field can operate. The government can make a great contribution in this field. What we really need, as we have been asking for a number of years, is for the government to accept its responsibilities. Then we could try to solve the problem. It seems to me the government must demonstrate that acceptance by creating a ministry-I know the constitutional difficulties that that might pose-of housing and urban affairs, headed by a full time minister.
Not another department?

I have been criticized in the house for the things I have said about the Prime Minister, but my remarks were not meant to be personal. The entire problem of housing is so immense, so critical and so national that it can only be solved, if it can be solved, by a minister who devotes his entire attention to it. Even if that were done I do not think we should solve our housing problems for a decade, we have been so neglectful and the problem has become so immense; but that would be a good start. I realize that at the conference the Prime Minister's suggestion that there should be a council was turned down by most of the provinces, but surely this poses a challenge to us here to give the kind of leadership which the people of this country so desperately want. It could be done, it seems to me, without infringing upon the constitution and without creating needless difficulties with the provinces.
[DOT] (10:50 a.m.)
The second thing we have to consider-and I am not sure we are capable of doing it-is this. We must take the position that the provision of adequate housing for the people of this country is as important as national defence. We think nothing of automatically providing in our estimates each year about $1.5 billion for national defence. Nobody minds. Nobody worries. Why not do the same for housing? Why not make the same effort to generate resources for the production of adequate accommodation for our people? I
(Mr. Scott (Danforth).]
propose that for the next five years we so reorganize our financial affairs as to provide $1.5 billion a year for the housing industry.
In order to provide this sum we ought to reorganize our forces. My God, if a war broke out anywhere we would have no trouble financing it; we would find the money somehow. Why not make the same kind of effort to house our people? I know the Prime Minister is going to leave us one of these days. Why not develop this new approach as a great centenary project? The right hon. gentleman would then really exit under full steam. For the first time let us in Ottawa do something properly; let us go all the way in an attempt to provide for our people. I know the minister will get up and announce all kinds of statistics, but this concerns people. We have reached a stage where any young persons marrying today will never own homes as long as they live.
Oh.

The minister of
national resources says "Oh". It is true. We have reached a point where both young and old do not have the housing they need. We have reached a point at which the National Housing Act helps only those earning more than $8,000 a year. It is not a national housing act but a national hoaxing act. It was designed to help the little man and it is not doing so.
We have been a complete and abject failure in the field of housing, and one of the best things we could do would be to admit it for a change and try to do something about it. I propose we should begin by providing $1.5 billion a year to help meet the needs of this industry. It would not meet all the need; I realize that, but I believe it is within our competence if we really want to make a national effort. The balance required would presumably come from private sources.
In lending this kind of money we should make sure it is made available for specific purposes. This is the way in which we could influence housing policy without interfering with the constitution. This is what is done at the present time. It is a trite phrase to say the C.M.H.C. are just mortgage brokers. Everyone knows that today by laying down conditions under which money will be lent the National Housing Act tremendously influences the types of houses which are built, their location, their services and everything connected with the housing field.
December 21, 1967

There is no reason for not carrying this further. Consider land prices. There is no hope of bringing down the cost of land except by land assembly on a massive basis. This could be done under our proposal. A strong initiative is needed in the work of rehabilitating our cities, and in urban development. This could come within the terms under which money is lent. Our failure in the public housing sector has been impressive; there are thousands of people in every city in the country waiting for public housing to be provided. This too could be a term under which money was lent. Housing for old people could also be influenced by the lending terms.
There is really no problem, Mr. Speaker. All that is required is a commitment, an acceptance of responsibility. Four years ago when I first spoke here on housing I said I envied the minister because with a little work he had it within his power to change the face of this country. He has been a failure, and unless he can make a pretty good speech today as far as I am concerned there is no hope for a solution of the housing problem with the present minister still in charge. I say this with considerable regret.
I wish to repeat in capsule form what I have said. The housing crisis constitutes the biggest social problem facing this nation. It is far greater than medicare; far greater than any other, even education. It must therefore be accepted as a matter for national concern, national responsibility and federal action. Second, the provinces are desperate for leadership. They do not object to federal initiative in this area. Having listened to the views expressed at the conference I believe there would be no difficulty about working out provincial agreements and regional programs. Third, there must be federal money available, and if the government wishes to make a commitment there is no reason for failure to find the money. It must be made available on a sustained basis. We must get away forever from the pump priming aspect and accept the opinion of the economic council that a wall must be erected around housing to protect it from the vicissitudes of the market. Until we accept this principle there is no hope of solving Canada's housing crisis.
We must take the initiative to demonstrate our sense or responsibility by creating a ministry of housing and urban affairs. Housing shortage is only a symptom. It is only the beginning of the nightmare of the urbanization of this country. We are not equipped for
Housing
it and we have no program to meet it. Yet in the next ten or 15 years all our people will live in the cities, and this will create problems of gigantic proportions. There is no point in rehashing the conference. The only time it really operated was when the Prime Minister was in charge. But these are the initiatives we have to take. If we do these things there is some chance in the field of housing. If we do not do them, it seems to me there is no hope.
How does one reach this government? How does one get through to it? I don't know; I have almost given up. But these are the things we must do. I hope this debate will impress upon the government both the tremendous social need and the tremendous urgency.
[DOT] (11:00 a.m.)

Mr. Speaker, we are dealing this morning with the housing problem, and this debate is limited to three hours. It has been going on for an hour and I am under the impression that we have not yet proposed some means likely to solve this crisis.
If the Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson), responsible for the administration of the National Housing Act before the house, has no other statement or suggestion to make than that which the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) made a few minutes ago, I think that we will solve very little today, in such a short debate and in view of the Prime Minister's statement.
The Prime Minister said that he wanted to create a federal-provincial council that would deal with housing. Mr. Speaker, there are already quite a number of those boards in various fields. There have been many federal, provincial and federal-provincial inquiries whose sole purpose was to keep the people from getting impatient and to postpone the solution of the problems.
The main reason for that housing crisis is a lack of money to build the houses our people need. I agree with Peter Newman who said in an editorial published in La Presse, on Saturday, May 6, 1967, that the trouble does not come from the fact that the construction industry cannot build enough houses but rather from the fact that credit is hard to get and the necessary funds are still in the hands of big financiers who prefer tc build commercial centres and office buildings. The individual who would like to obtain a

December 21, 1967
Housing
loan to build a house is unable to find assistance in financial quarters. Mr. Speaker, I think that it is exactly the point.
A tew weeks ago, the government raised the rate of interest for loans granted under the National Housing Act from 71 per cent -which was already quite high-to 8J per cent, apparently to encourage capitalists to consider the housing problem and to make funds available to builders for the construction of houses. Well, if that was the government's purpose, it did not materialize because what happened was exactly the opposite. The capitalists may have more funds, but can the borrowers commit themselves for 25 or 30 years at such a high rate of interest?
People are thinking seriously before committing themselves, and the demand in the field of housing construction is growing smaller. The solution, in my opinion, would be for the government, through the Bank of Canada, to make credit available to the provinces which request it-the consensus of opinion at the federal-provincial conference on housing was that the provinces want to deal with their housing problems themselves -at a low rate of interest. Those who want to buy a house would then be able to make their monthly payments and pay a reasonable interest rate. Moreover, they could perhaps repay their debt within 15 to 20 years instead of 30 to 35 years and save a considerable amount of money, which would encourage those who want to own their home. As the situation now stands, obviously, it is almost impossible for an individual to buy a house, whatever his age, and to commit himself to pay for it over a period of 25, 30 and 35 years, for it is quite clear that he will never really own his house.
As a result, Mr. Speaker, I think that if the government really intends to solve the housing problem, the first thing would be to make available to the population, at a low interest rate, the necessary credit to encourage home ownership.
When I mention those who have no home, I am thinking precisely of those who would like to purchase a house and who must pay rent. They have a roof over their head, it is true, but the roof does not belong to them and they may be forced at any time to leave such housing for other accommodation which will not belong to them either.
It is clear Mr. Speaker, and social science admits it today, that each family is entitled

to its house and that the role of the government is precisely to see to it that this purpose is achieved.
There is another point I would like to bring up also. It was emphasized by Michael Wheeler in a speech to the annual conference of mayors and municipalities held in Montreal on July 24, 1967. Mr. Wheeler precisely dealt with a very important point nowadays concerning the municipality wishing to develop housing projects. This is precisely what he says:
Promoters and developers are annoyed by the long delays in land development and the allegedly extravagant standards imposed upon them.
From my own experience, the problems of the small town where I live are the same as those of large cities. New housing projects are needed, but since municipalities cannot afford to undertake them, they must borrow to do so.
All those standards imposed on them result in long delays. For some houses built in our area, we had to fight, so to speak, with the C.M.H.C. I must admit that officials of that corporation have been very understanding and I would not say they have eluded the regulations of the corporation, but almost. Had it not been that those civil servants were most understanding, some forty or fifty houses would not have been built in the municipality of LaSarre. They have now been built thanks to them. Here again, I feel that if the government wanted to be efficient, it would give the municipalities easier access to credit, at low interest rates, so that as soon as requests are made for housing developments, they might give the necessary services to ready them for the new owners.
Here is another important way in which the housing problem might be solved: the cost of houses should go down and the first step towards that would be to remove the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials. This would lower construction costs considerably and thus encourage more working people to own their own home.
Sometimes, the government or other agencies call for the construction of low-cost housing units for low-income citizens. Mr. Speaker, I object to the use of the term "low-cost" to describe the units offered to disadvantaged people. In view of our building materials and labour costs today, it is not possible to build low-cost dwellings that are adequate and fit for human beings.
December 21, 1967

There is a considerable number of slum dwellings in our cities, towns and rural communities. To build low-cost houses that are financially acceptable to disadvantaged people, we would have to build slums. However, these slums are already too numerous, and there is no need to build more or new ones. Needy people, those in the lower income brackets deserve and have a right to live in comfortable and decent houses, and we should see to it that they do.
Some also want to encourage more people to own their home. There is another reason only eventual owners hesitate to make long-range commitments: the taxes they have to pay. That is an important point which many think about, in my opinion quite rightly.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
To correct that anomaly, several suggestions were made during this session. In fact, one of my colleagues presented a motion providing that individuals purchasing or owning a house be allowed to deduct the amount of school or municipal taxes which they have to pay from their income tax. So, as supplementary taxes seem to be levied all the time, I think that only one tax at a time should be imposed, so that people can become home-owners more easily.
I think that the federal government should authorize any Canadian citizen who buys a new one-family dwelling for himself to deduct the property taxes in full for income tax purposes. In my opinion, he should get an exemption for the following expenditures, or rather he should deduct from his taxable income the amount paid on the price of the house and land, including the municipal and school taxes, as well as the monthly mortgage payments, including the interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: For how long?

Until the house is fully paid for.
In my opinion, such steps would enable Canadians to become quickly the owners of their home without mortgaging part of their income. We know that 100 per cent of the income of most workers, whether they are labourers, miners, lumbermen or workers in the construction field or any other industry and service, goes to discharge the monthly instalments on their house, to purchase furniture or any other item or to pay medical fees. We know that municipal taxes and especially school taxes are liable to go up, I would say, almost every year. Each tax increase means a
Housing
decrease of income for the taxpayer and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) recently raised the income tax by 5 per cent. That new increase creates problems for those people because, with a decrease of income, and mortgaged as they are up to the hilt, they cannot meet their numerous payments.
Therefore, I think that steps should be taken to prevent those too frequent increases and I am of the opinion that exemptions on capital expenses of a house would be welcome by the people. Furthermore, if the present Prime Minister took measures of this kind before he leaves the leadership of his party, I am sure that this would meet the wish expressed earlier by the hon. member of Danforth (Mr. Scott), I think, when he said that the Prime Minister would leave the leadership of his party under very favourable conditions, and it would help his successor in his task if he solved that problem.
Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to prolong the debate any further and will close my remarks with the few recommendations made to the Minister of Labour on November 20, 1967. I am referring to the recommendations of the National House Builders Association and more specifically to the most interesting points that warrant mention, and should be recalled to the readers of Hansard, and I quote:
1.	Lower the initial amount required to buy a house.
2.	Reduce the monthly charges required from the purchaser of a house.
3.	Reduce N.H.A. mortgage insurance fees and mortgage application costs to a reasonable level.
4.	Eliminate the 11 per cent federal sales tax on building materials or pay back the same amount to the home buyer, with provincial governments taking similar steps where needed.
5.	Facilitate private and public financing for a greater number of rental dwellings.
6.	Ease the terms under which limited dividend homes could be built for low-income families.
7.	Find new ways of eliminating high costs of land development, and reducing education financing and community services.
8.	Remove all impediments that delay, at this time, the approval of land zoning plans, so as to provide an adequate number of serviced building lots.
Recommendation No. 8 agrees with a statement given by Mr. Wheeler during his speech before the municipal authorities in Montreal, last July.
9.	Establish uniform building standards and regulations.
Mr. Speaker, I think those recommendations should be thoroughly considered by the

December 21, 1967
Housing
government, and on the occasion of future federal-provincial conferences, I believe all levels of government would be able to enter into adequate agreements to ensure the welfare of all the Canadian people, in brief, of all future Canadian home-owners, e (11:20 a.m.)

Mr. Speaker, it has been alleged that the recent housing conference would not bring about the construction of one additional house. I have been wondering whether the debate today will be any more effective in this regard than was the recent conference. In recent times we have had a number of debates in the house on this important question, many questions have been raised on orders of the day, the matter has been constantly brought to the attention of the government and we have been reminding ourselves of its importance, but we still find ourselves in a very difficult situation as far as housing in Canada is concerned.
Food, clothing and shelter are the three basic needs of man, and of course in this debate we are dealing with the third. There has been a growing awareness in the past several years that we would be faced with a serious problem in the area of housing, but as usual the governments concerned waited until the problem reached crisis proportions before making any really earnest attempt to face and try to resolve it.
It is our contention that if positive measures had been taken in the way of monetary and fiscal policies we would not be in the position we are in today. But this was not done, and today we find ourselves in the position of once again discussing this important issue. It has been described as our worst crisis since the depression. This observation was made by Professor A. J. Diamond of the University of Toronto school of architecture. When we view the problem from this angle it should spur us on to the realization that if we are in any way to meet the challenge of the next few years there is no time to be lost; we must move forward with resolution and determination. Even though measures taken may be out of the ordinary, I believe circumstances develop from time to time that make it absolutely necessary to take such measures.
There is no need this morning to discuss the importance of adequate housing to the people of our country. This has been dealt with in various debates in the past. After all,

I think it is one of the basic rights of our people to have access to adequate housing. Housing has a tremendous impact as far as the social problems which face us are concerned. I believe all of us recognize the importance of Canadians having adequate housing. It has also been placed on record on a number of occasions that the housing situation today is very serious. It has been indicated that in order to meet the need in this area, 160,000 or more housing units are required each year. This is necessitated by increased immigration, by the formation of new family units and by the necessity of replacing obsolete and inadequate housing. I believe that substantially more than 160,000 units will be required to adequately meet the problem in the days that lie ahead.
A great many families are living in substandard units today. Many families are living in units that are far too small for the size of the family. In fact, it has been pointed out in recent communications and news articles that some families have no housing unit of any kind. I think this is a deplorable situation in a country that is so blessed with material goods, with everything that is necessary for the construction of adequate housing units. Depite this we find people living in types of accommodation that are far beneath the dignity of any individual in any part of the world.
The United Church of Canada, at page 163 of a book entitled "Canada and its Future", published an article dealing with housing. I should like to read part of it as follows:
Canada's housing program, both public and private, is a failure. Experts have different opinions on what to do about it. But almost all of them- public enterprisers, private enterprisers and middle of the readers-agree that the housing program has failed in the following ways:-
I shall indicate what the various paragraphs contain. They are as follows;
Housing construction is falling behind the population increase.
Housing is not being built fast enough to substantially reduce the backlog of slums and overcrowded dwellings.
Decent housing is too costly for an increasing number of middle income families and poor families.
Public housing exists for only a fraction of the low income families that need it.
At the 1961 census, an estimated 923,000 Canadian households were lodged in broken down, crowded or unsanitary houses or were straining their budgets to the limit and running into debt in order to pay the rent.
December 21, 1967

I think this is a sad commentary on the housing situation in a country that has been so signally blessed by Providence. It has been suggested that this is not the time to lay blame on any government or agency, but a time when we ought to try to face the problem objectively and realistically and come up with some satisfactory answers. I suggest it is rather difficult to do this in the light of the government's record with regard to housing.
I have stated before in debate that the present government has subscribed to the concept that every Canadian should have the right to live in his own home, or have accommodation that is adequate for his needs, but again we find that the government has been working against itself in trying to implement this philosophy. On one occasion, even though it was to serve another purpose altogether, the government introduced the winter incentive program whereby those who had homes built in the winter months received a bonus of $500. This program had a very salutary effect upon our housing picture, a great many people availed themselves of this provision and had homes built during the winter. However, not very long after this program was introduced the government imposed the 11 per cent sales tax on building materials, which more than offset the $500 winter bonus program.
Then just recently measures were introduced which permitted the interest rate on N.H.A. loans to rise to a maximum of 8J per cent. It was pointed out that this would have a beneficial effect in making more mortgage money available for housing. It may have had some such effect, but as far as expert advice is concerned it has not resulted in any appreciable difference in the availability of mortgage money.
[DOT] (11:30 a.m.)
In addition the increase in mortgage rates, which we are now told is reaching the maximum, has placed housing beyond the capacity of a great majority of Canadian citizens. So we find that the 11 per cent sales tax, interest rates which are constantly rising, and increased municipal taxes all put together are forcing a great many home owners to sell their houses because they believe it is far more economical to rent accommodation than to build and own homes.
So we find that our policies are working against each other, and instead of achieving the desired result and meeting the need the situation is improving very little, if at all.
Housing
It has been pointed out that the great need in this particular area is for money. I do not think there is any shortage of lumber or other types of building materials. As my hon. friend from Vancouver East indicated, there is a surplus of lumber in British Columbia and we who are from that province know this. So it is a matter of money and I believe, in spite of what has been said in days gone by about the necessity of cutting down on expenditures priorities must be established. I do not think we should economize in an area such as housing, which is so important to the welfare of Canadians.
My colleague the hon. member for Red Deer, speaking in debate on October 2 here in the house, pointed out the necessity of establishing a far larger revolving fund. He was checked by the Minister of Labour, who said this had been done. My colleague went on to state that it had to be vastly expanded if it was to meet the particular need at this time. I believe a fund should be established which would provide the necessary capital to enable Canadians from coast to coast, if they so desire, to build their own homes and enjoy the security which only home ownership can give. Some incentives must be provided. The first would be to make capital available at reasonable rates of interest. This was pointed out by my colleague from Red Deer in the speech to which I referred. I would like to quote his statement because I think it is important. This is what he said:
Even at 7 per cent, Mr. Speaker, a $12,000 mortgage, which we will say is the average mortgage for the average home, will in 20 years cost the home owner more than $10,000 by way of interest, or a total of $22,000. In 30 years the interest charge alone is more than $16,000, or a total of $28,500. But when one takes the present rate of 81 per cent one finds that in 20 years a $12,000 mortgage will cost $13,000 more than the cost of the home itself, or a total in excess of $25,000. In 30 years the cost of the $12,000 mortgage at 81 per cent, will exceed the cost of the home by $18,000 or a total cost of more than $30,000.
There is something drastically wrong when in order to build and own a home a Canadian citizen must pay the value of his home two or three times over because of interest charges. Either there is something drastically wrong with our legislation dealing with rates of interest or there is something drastically wrong with an economy which forces our people to mortgage 30 or 40 years of their future in order to own their own homes, by which time most of them are so old they do not enjoy them for very long.

December 21, 1967
Housing
We have operated on monetary and fiscal policies in Canada which penalize our people to the point of desperation. So, as I said, we must provide as an incentive some way of obtaining money at reasonable rates of interest, and this should be one of the major concerns of the government at this time. Think about lower income families having to buy homes under these circumstances. I suggest that housing should not be considered as ather forms of investment such as commercial investments, and so on, because it vitally effects the welfare and health of our people.
I suggest also that there should be an incentive in the form of grants to those who desire to build their own homes. I have before me the British Columbia Government News of January and February, 1967 in which the budget of British Columbia is discussed. I should like to read from this article one of the highlights of the budget, namely:
Home acquisition grant fund of $25 million set up. The individual grant to be $500 retroactive to April 1, 1966.
So the province is setting up a fund of $25 million called the home acquisition grant fund from which individuals can obtain grants of $500 in order to assist them in home construction and home purchase.
In his statement this morning the Prime Minister referred to the possibility of subsidization in the future by granting some type of assistance to those in lower income brackets for the purchase of homes, particularly in areas of slow economic growth. That is all very well, but I think people should have access to some form of grant no matter where they live, and I suggest that $1,000 or even $2,000 would not be too much for this purpose and would be a good investment so far as the Canadian nation is concerned.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would he not agree that in effect the proposal of the British Columbia government for a home acquisition grant fund might be considered to be a refund of the sales tax which the government has already collected from prospective home owners?
Does the hon. member mean the 11 per cent sales tax?
No, the British Columbia 5 per cent tax.

I should like to point out that the money to which the hon. member for Comox-Alberni referred is used to cover the

cost of the hospitalization program. We have a hospitalization program there for which the people pay no premiums directly. The sales tax is used for that specific purpose, as well as other revenues, and all the people of British Columbia are very happy to have that program at this time.
[DOT] (11:40 a.m.)
I suggest also, Mr. Speaker, that in order to assist those who are desirous of having their own homes there should be a depreciation allowance applicable to income tax. This provision is made in so far as business and industrial properties are concerned. If the principle is applicable in those particular areas, why could it not apply to home ownership? I think this is desirable and necessary. I believe it is something that is warranted. We urge the Minister of National Revenue therefore to take this particular suggestion into consideration and endeavour to devise a provision that will permit home owners to enjoy the privileges enjoyed by others in the form of depreciation allowances.
Now, Mr. Speaker, there are many others who would like to speak today, and although there are many other things we would like to see done we do not want to monopolize the time. We do want to impress upon the government once again the importance of this issue, not that they are not aware of it. However, we hope the government will be able to do something positive by way of a solution to encourage home ownership in Canada and provide more adequately for the housing needs of Canadians. I hope the suggestions that have been made will receive careful consideration.

Mr. Speaker, those of us on this side of the house recognize, of course, that we have a housing problem in Canada. We recognize our responsibility to deal effectively with it. In his remarks the Prime Minister outlined certain of the new initiatives which we are taking to meet the housing problem. The fact that the Prime Minister intervened in this debate indicates how seriously we on this side take this particular problem. In view of the fact that the debate was demanded by the opposition parties it strikes me as a bit peculiar that the Leader of the Opposition and the leader of the New Democratic party have not seen fit to attach the same importance to the subject as the Prime Minister has done.

We have ability all round.
December 21, 1967

Of course we have a housing problem in Canada. We have a housing problem because in Canada we are growing rapidly. People are flocking to Canada from every part of the world. Our problems, Mr. Speaker, and our housing problem in particular are problems which arise from rapid growth. This is a problem of success. It is very different from the problem which faced members of the opposition when they formed the government. At that time they had no housing probem. The population was not growing rapidly. They had the problem of mass unemployment. They had the problems of economic slowdown. Their problems were problems of failure, not problems of success.
Naturally we would prefer not to have any problems. However, if we have to have problems we on this side of the house would much prefer to face problems arising from our success rather than from our failure. The housing problem we have today in Canada arises from the fact that we have a successful and expanding economy in Canada. People are flocking to this country from every country in the world. During the year 1967 over 200,000 immigrants will have come to Canada. This is quite a different situation from the one which faced members of the opposition when they formed the government.
We are aware of the problem and we accept our responsibility to deal effectively with it. During recent months those of us in this house who represent ridings in metropolitan. Toronto have become more and more alarmed at the rapid build-up of the housing crisis in our own area. I believe I can speak for most Toronto members when I say we have a serious housing crisis there. I don't apologize for using the word "crisis", because that is exactly the right word. Nor do I apologize for emphasizing the situation in Toronto. It is merely an example of the problem which we face in all our large urban areas. It is a problem of national magnitude resulting from our success and an expanding economy.
I do not want to deal in generalities, Mr. Speaker, but in hard facts. In this perhaps I differ from the hon. member for Danforth, who preferred to avoid statistics and instead, in sanctimonious and dismayed tones, levelled harsh and unfair charges unembarrassed by any consideration of our real accomplishments in this field. I prefer, Mr. Speaker, to deal in hard facts, not in unjust accusations.
The hard fact is that at the present time in Toronto, due to our economic success and
Housing
growth, there is just no housing accommodation available. Our actual vacancy rate in Toronto is at the unbelievably low rate of 1 per cent, the lowest vacancy rate in North America. Our metropolitan Toronto housing registry has 11,000 families on its waiting list, and that number is rising at the rate of 1,500 families per quarter. Yesterday, in this Christmas season, there were ten families including 35 children living in the city's emergency family hostel. At this time last year there was one family. In Toronto city proper

I am not speaking of metro Toronto-out of 185,000 housing units we have only 2,400 housing units geared to income, that is to say, public housing units. A recommended percentage is 8 per cent of the total, or about five times as many as we now have. Since 1962 the city of Toronto proper has built and acquired less than 1,200 housing units geared to income.
In the metro area outside the city proper the record is much better, but far from good enough. In June 1964 there was an accumulated stock of 2,310 geared to income family units. This figure does not include housing for the elderly or student housing. In 1965 we increased this stock by almost 1,100 units. In 1966 the increase was about 1,634 units and in 1967 to date over 1,300 units, for a total increase during the three year period of over 4,000 units. In addition we have under construction over 5,000 units; we have completed loan commitments for 293 and commitments are in process for an additional 635 for a total of 5,955 additional public housing units.
We are doing a great deal, but we have a long way to go to meet our objectives. No one on this side of the house has ever denied that fact. My point is this, Mr. Speaker. Although it is not usually recognized, by far the greater part of this public housing to which I have referred was built under the provision of our National Housing Act under which the federal government pays 90 per cent of the capital cost and undertakes to pay 50 per cent of any operating deficits.
Big deal.

It is quite clear that the federal government has borne by far the largest financial responsibility in this field. As members of the opposition have said, it is a big deal and it is a good deal. We believe it is right that the federal government should bear this responsibility in this field. Canada is not a group of independent provinces,

December 21, 1967
Housing
loosely federated. It is a modern, dynamic, young but rapidly growing nation which must have a national housing policy. The Toronto housing crisis is not caused by local conditions or by internal growth. As I have said, people are flocking to Toronto from every part of Ontario, from every part of Canada, from every part of the world. During the last six years one quarter of all immigrants to Canada have come to metropolitan Toronto. No wonder we have a housing problem, Mr. Speaker.
[DOT] (11:50 a.m.)
Clearly this problem cannot be solved entirely at the municipal or the provincial level. We recognize our responsibility and are doing something about it. The housing problem in Toronto, I repeat, is not a local problem, nor is it an isolated problem. It is just one aspect of the national, indeed the global problem with which we have to cope resulting from the inevitable growth of great urban areas. Such development gives rise not only to housing problems but to the closely related problems of the disposal of sewage and waste products and the pollution of water and air.
All these, Mr. Speaker, are major problems which result from our rapid growth which in turn stems from the very success of our efforts in Canada. It has been estimated by some that by the end of this century almost half of Canada's population will live within 50 miles of Toronto and Montreal unless effective action is taken to stop the present trend.
Would the hon. member permit a question. If the housing crisis cannot be solved in good times, when will it be solved?

Mr. Speaker, that question really does not make much sense. We are making rapid progress and we will continue to make rapid progress. The facts I have mentioned make it entirely clear that there is a certain federal responsibility for housing and that we must have a national housing policy. But we cannot overlook the fact that the provinces and the municipalities have their responsibilities as well.
Would the hon. member permit a question. Are we to take it from his remarks that what he is really saying is that we are all so prosperous that we cannot afford housing?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the hon. member for Danforth recognizes that that is not the proper interpretation to put upon my remarks. There is a clear federal responsibility in the field but, as I say, we cannot overlook the fact that the provinces and the municipalities have their responsibilities as well, and we cannot completely disregard them.
In the last housing debate in this house in September the hon. member for Brome-Mis-sisquoi and the hon. member for Danforth, who participated again today, urged us to proceed full speed ahead. There would be no difficulty in getting co-operation from the provinces, they said. As reported at page 2611 of Hansard, when referring to the policy of his own party, the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi had this to say:
There was also no doubt in our minds that housing was a national consideration and concern-
Let us be clear now that while we require the co-operation of the provinces and the municipalities the ultimate responsibility for housing, or the lack of it, rests with the federal authority.
What did the hon. member for Danforth say, Mr. Speaker? In prophesying what would be the attitude of the provinces he had this to say, as reported at page 2597 of Hansard:
Housing is of national concern-
I agree with that.
-no matter under whose jurisdiction it lies. The people in the provincial governments are eager to co-operate with the federal government. They are looking for help, leadership and co-operation. They are not worried about the B.N.A. Act; they are worried about their people.
Since that time, Mr. Speaker, we have had federal-provincial co-operation, and what false prophets hon. members opposite have proved to be. The provincial leaders were anxious to co-operate all right; they were anxious to co-operate in receiving federal funds but not prepared to tolerate any further federal initiatives in the field of housing.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of privilege.
Mr. Speaker, I will be prepared to answer any questions-
I am rising on a point of privilege.
