Mr. Speaker, I cannot permit that type of distortion to remain on Hansard.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. There is no point of privilege about a disagreement of fact. The hon. member for St. Paul's.

With great respect, Mr. Speaker, it is not a matter of fact. The hon. member has quoted a previous speech of mine and has placed a completed distorted construction upon it. Surely that is a matter of privilege. He quoted a previous remark of mine to the effect that the provincial governments came to the conference in an uncooperative manner. That I have never said. We all know, even if the government will not admit it, that the conference died because there was no leadership from the government.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. The hon.
member for St. Paul's.

Mr. Speaker, I should merely like to point out that I did not say the provincial leaders came to the conference in an unco-operative mood. On the contrary, I said they came to the conference prepared to co-operate and to accept federal funds, but not to tolerate any further federal initiatives in the field of housing. I think that is a statement of fact. I sat through the conference.
In the result, Mr. Speaker, it is entirely clear that the federal government was right in its decision to concentrate available federal housing money in areas of greatest need. In 1968, as announced at the conference, there will be no federal money for speculative building but federal money will be increased by $150 million over 1967 in the areas of greatest need, that is to say in the areas of housing for students and senior citizens, limited dividend housing under a new limited dividend housing policy, urban renewal and, most important of all at the present time, public housing.
The hon. member for Danforth urged what might be called a five or six point program of which the main proposal seemed to be the establishment of a new department of housing affairs. There may be some merit, Mr. Speaker, in setting up a new department of housing, but at the present time I do not think a new department of housing would add a single housing unit to our housing stock. We have a crisis, and more effective 27053-360
Housing
action is needed than the creation of an additional department at additional public expense.
Federal money will be available for public housing. As has been pointed out on numerous occasions, no legitimate application for public housing funds has ever been refused by C.M.H.C. More money will be available for that purpose this coming year than in 1967. But that is not enough. The federal government must continue in the future, as it has in the past, to develop new initiatives and programs. The Prime Minister outlined certain of these which are now proposed. We must induce the provinces and municipalities to use effectively the money, which certainly is available, to provide the housing which we in Canada undoubtedly need at the present time.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to take up a very short time because there are a number of members of the house who desire to speak and to make useful contributions. I will speak for but a few moments.
The Prime Minister told us that by the end of this year we can expect to have made no more than 160,000 housing starts. According to Dominion Bureau of Statistics figures, during the second quarter of this year the number of housing starts was at a seasonally adjusted rate of 192,000 for the year. In the third quarter of this year the number of housing starts was down to 178,000 for the year, seasonally adjusted. We have now dropped to 160,000 on the admission of the Prime Minister this morning. In other words, in the past six months housing starts have been reduced by 17 per cent. The number will be 4,000 less than two years ago. The hon. member for St. Paul's has just told us that the government was making progress. It seems that the Liberal government's idea of progress, Mr. Speaker, is to construct less and less and less and less housing.
[DOT] (12 noon)
These figures represent a shameful admission of failure on the part of the government. This is no more than a housing policy in reverse. We are going steadily backward. We shall produce at least 30,000 fewer houses than the minimum number the Economic Council of Canada has said should be produced in order to provide for the housing needs of Canada in one year. We shall, because we are going in reverse so far as house production is concerned at the present

December 21, 1967
Housing
time, produce less than 160,000 houses next year.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
At the end of my remarks I shall.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: At the end of the speech.

At the end of my speech I shall permit questions. When the Prime Minister spoke this morning he tried to minimize the catastrophe which the housing conference two weeks ago was. It is well known that the cabinet was divided on whether a conference on housing should be called. Many in the cabinet believed that the conference should be held at the officials' level and that there was not sufficient information to pass along to the provincial premiers for a full-fledged conference involving the Prime Minister, the provincial premiers and federal government ministers to be called.
The Minister of Labour (Mr. Nicholson) persuaded the cabinet that the conference should be held. Typical of the descriptions of this conference, which appeared in nearly all the newspapers of this country, was the one written by Mr. John Dafoe in the December 15 issue of the Globe and Mail. The column is headed, "The Housing Talks Fizzled While Homeowners Burned". I shall read only the first paragraph because it describes the situation adequately:
This week's federal-provincial conference on housing probably came closest to producing unanimous agreement of any conference in recent memory. Almost everybody agreed that it was a flop.
Then he describes in detail what kind of flop it was and why it was a serious mistake to have called the conference in the first place. In my opinion, the speech which the Prime Minister delivered at that conference must have been prepared by someone who works in the Department of Labour. The Prime Minister must have delivered it without having read it first; otherwise I do not think he would have made the speech. It was not a speech that an intelligent man would have made.
At the end the main suggestion for solving the housing crisis was that another committee should be formed, another consultative council which from time to time would report to the provincial premiers and provincial governments and advise them of the housing situation. The provincial premiers who came here, Mr. Speaker, are fully conversant with

the housing problems of their provinces. They wanted leadership from the federal government. They wanted to hear the government's housing policy. These busy men took time out from their other duties to come to the conference, and when they got to it they heard the Prime Minister say that the problem would be solved by appointing yet another committee. This is a government of committees, Mr. Speaker.
And task forces.

This government does not know how to make decisions. It has had a committee deliberating a matter that has been discussed by many other Canadians for the past five or six years. I refer to the question of foreign investment. That committee cannot make up its mind. At some time in the future we will hear the result of the deliberations of yet another committee.
When the provincial premiers heard the Prime Minister make his speech that day- and I talked to a number of them-they did not know whether to laugh or cry. It was the most pathetic performance, they said, that they had seen in many a long year at Ottawa. This is the kind of performance we are getting from this government. It is inexcusable having this kind of flop with respect to housing; in fact, it is very serious indeed. But it would have been a catastrophe if such a fiasco had been perpetrated on the busy premiers who spent three or four days at that most important conference which took place in Toronto, a conference conducted under the auspices of the premier of Ontario, a conference that will produce something concrete. These busy premiers came here hoping for an answer to the housing crisis and they got absolutely nothing.
When the conference ended on the second of its proposed three days, only two of the ten premiers were still in attendance. The second day of the conference was like the second night of a bad play when there are very few people in attendance.
Hear, hear.

The housing conference was a fiasco. What we in the opposition are afraid of is that if the housing conference could be such a flop, what will happen to that conference which is to be held at the beginning of February to deal with the most important matter that this country has probably ever dealt with, the constitutional crisis. If at the coming conference we see evidence of the
December 21, 1967

same lack of preparation as was evident in the housing conference and if fatuous speeches are made by ministers of the government, the constitutional conference will prove to be a calamity from which this country may never recover. I say to the government, for heaven's sake, pull up your socks. Act like a government. Stop perpetrating fiasco after fiasco on this country. Let us see some leadership or, for heaven's sake, move over and let others who can give leadership take office.
May I ask a question?

I shall be glad to answer all questions a little later, Mr. Speaker. I should like to continue my remarks, if you do not mind, sir.
I want to say a word about our two northern territories. When the Prime Minister spoke this morning he said, quite rightly, that a great deal of the responsibility for housing rests on the shoulders of the provinces. They carry out the actual policies. Our two northern territories face a grave housing crisis, as grave as that in any province. The territories were not even invited to the housing conference. They wanted to be invited but because of problems of jurisdiction they were left out. That was one of the results of calling a conference without being better prepared to deal with the subject. The government did not have the courtesy and good sense to invite to the housing conference representatives from our two northern territories in order that they might inform the government of the problems of the territories and in order that the government might become conversant with the housing problems there. I say that those territories ought to have been represented at such a conference in order to have been able to bring forward their problems.
One of the principal difficulties facing house construction is the high cost of money as represented by high interest rates. This government must get its financial house in order, control its expenditures and restore public confidence.
Hear, hear.

What is the record of the government in this regard? Since taking office just four and a half years ago the government has increased government expenditures by no less than $3 billion, or 47 per cent. That is a fantastic performance in overspending the public's money. The government has had to go to the bond market many 27053-3601
Housing
times, far more often than any government in the past. The Canadian people have seen the government returning time and again to the bond market and have held back from buying the bonds that the government has issued from time to time. Members of the public have known full well that if they wait for the next issue or the one after that they will be able to demand a higher rate of interest on the money they lend. This has driven interest rates up. It has made mortgage money in short supply. It has driven building costs up and made it almost impossible for many Canadians to obtain the housing they need.
What has the government done to put its financial house in order and to cope with this situation? It has done absolutely nothing. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) the other day told us several times that he intended to bring about drastic cuts in the present budget. I am speaking of the 1967-68 budget. He told me that when the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Benson) spoke he would announce what cuts were to be made. You and I know, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of National Revenue did not mention once in his speech any cut that the government intended to make in its 1967-68 budget. What was said by the Minister of Finance was a complete misrepresentation of the facts. Nothing in that regard has been done up to the present time. Nothing is being done to cut expenditures between now and when the next budget is presented in April.
We have the ludicrous assurance by the government that they intend to take the extraordinary step of cutting $1.2 billion from government expenditures. Every member in this house who has served as a minister knows that when a budget is prepared every department brings forward everything that it wishes to do for the public. They are all good and desirable measures. They place them before Treasury Board and then it is determined whether the government can afford to carry out all these measures at that time. Invariably the government cuts off about $1 billion in proposed expenditures because there is not enough money to do everything. This is nothing new. The government has done nothing new.

It is a fraud.
* (12:10 p.m.)

It is simply fraud. The government has done nothing to cut real expenditures or to restore public confidence in its financial responsibility. As an example, in

December 21. 1967
Housing
the first seven months of this year-and these are the only available figures-the government has increased expenditures by no less than 15 per cent. I say in conclusion-
Hear, hear.

Yes, I realize that hon. members on the other side are glad to hear that I am about to finish my speech because they do not like what I am saying. As the old saying goes, it's music to the gambler's ears to hear the suckers roar. That is what they are doing, and it is music to my ears. They do not like what I am saying because I am telling them a few hard truths. I say, let the government get its house in order, cut expenditures, revive confidence, bring interest rates down as a result, and enable the Canadian people to acquire the houses they need to put over their heads.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. R. Nicholson (Minister of Labour):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I must say that I heartily welcomed this debate in the hope, perhaps unwarranted, that not only constructive criticism but some constructive suggestions would be forthcoming. As I have said more than once, I think criticism is necessary on occasion and that where warranted it should be forthcoming without any punches being pulled; it should come not only from the opposition but from the news media and any other sources which can make worth-while contributions.
In the light of the actual facts, however, I must say I have been perturbed not only by the nature of some of the debate which has taken place this morning but by some of the press comments which followed the housing conference. Some of the criticism may well have been justified. The conference probably would not have been a success if some criticism had not emerged. On the other hand, after hearing views loudly voiced by people who were not at the conference and by others who did not take the time to inform themselves adequately of the facts, I think it might be prudent at the outset of my remarks to refer briefly to the reasons the recent conference was held and the nature and extent of what actually took place there, so that these matters can be kept in proper perspective and adequately set down in the records of this house.
Was Premier Robarts not at that conference?

Yes, he was, and I shall have something to say about that in a

moment. Last March, speaking about the importance of inter-governmental co-operation in all branches of governmental activity, the Prime Minister had occasion to refer to housing. He said at that time:
This is an area where the primary constitutional responsibility for action lies with the provincial and municipal governments, but in which all governments must work together.
He then went on to say:
Certainly the federal government cannot ignore the rising dissatisfaction among Canadians with our urban environment not only as to the availability of adequate housing for everyone but as to the human equality of our community development.
Hon. members will also recall that in the speech from the throne read in May it was announced that the federal government proposed to consult with the provinces on problems and prospects in connection with housing and urban development. The conference was called against this background. The Prime Minister has referred to the letter which went out to the provincial premiers inviting them to meet to discuss problems of mutual interest. These invitations were extended to provide for the first time in Canada's history an opportunity for an exchange of views on this critical and, perhaps I should say, very sensitive subject. This was the objective of the conference and it was so set out clearly in the letters of invitation which went to the provincial premiers.
Not all governments received them.

All provinces received
them. The conference was designed to stress the need to pool our thinking in planning for the future and this was made clear in the advance publicity. It was pointed out that money was not the only consideration but that other major problems were involved and other challenges had to be met if we were to make urban Canada the attractive environment we would wish to see.
This becomes all the more urgent when we realize, as has been stated in this house more than once, that within a relatively few years, 12 or 13 I believe, 80 per cent of the people of this country will be living in fewer than 30 city or metropolitan areas and that one-third of the people will be living in three metropolitan areas. In these circumstances we thought it was about time that a conference on housing and related matters should take place.
December 21, 1967

Unfortunately, since that conference there has been a great deal of loose talk and loose writing about the premature termination of those meetings and a certain provincial premier walking out. Remarks of this sort were made this morning by the hon. member for Northumberland (Mr. Hees), who does not know what he is talking about because he was not there. The conference did not collapse. On the morning the conference opened, the Prime Minister was advised by at least two of the heads of provincial delegations that they hoped it would be possible for them to get away on the evening of the second day rather than have the conference extend to a third day. With this in mind we extended the length of the sessions on both days. On Monday we not only sat until 5.30 in the afternoon but we also had a very important evening meeting which was not on the original agenda. At that meeting we discussed housing in rural areas, one of the items which would normally have been discussed on the second day. The hours were also extended on the second day. By agreement the conference opened at 9.30 a.m. and we sat until about 7.20 p.m. in line with the expressed wish of heads of delegations.
[DOT] (12:20 pjn.)
The suggestion that all premiers walked out is absolutely absurd. One provincial premier did walk out but I understand he walked out to revise notes he had prepared. They were quite different from the ones he tabled at the beginning of the conference. I say the conference did not end prematurely. It ended having sat roughly the same number of hours that were originally contemplated would be spent and it ended with a very useful discussion in which the leaders of some of the provincial delegations who had a special interest in rural housing took part. The conference sat until approximately 7.20 p.m. on the second day. The premier of Nova Scotia had to leave about 6.30 because he had an appointment with the Prime Minister, but he took an active and helpful part in the discussion until he left. The representatives of Newfoundland and British Columbia, the premier of Prince Edward Island-they were all there as well as others taking part in the discussions.
It is more important, in my opinion, to talk about what was actually accomplished than it is to talk about failure or collapse. There were two concrete, positive achievements at the conference. First, as mentioned by the
Housing
Prime Minister this morning, there was general agreement among all ten provinces with the four broad and very significant proposals put forward by the government of Canada in its wish to assist in meeting the long-range challenges that confront us. These four items will appear in Hansard, since they were referred to by the Prime Minister in his remarks this morning. The second one, however, federal financial support for land assembly and development of comprehensively planned new suburban communities within urban regions, warrants a supplementary word because we are making progress in this very important field.
In answer to a question put to me in the house on Monday I referred to the very effective work being carried on by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation and the Ontario Housing Corporation in the development of a federal-provincial land tract at Malvern. This is a very strategically located and valuable tract of land, and the project shows what can be done if federal-provincial partnerships are to be effective. It has a potential of a highly desirable community of 30,000 or perhaps 32,000 people, with schools, churches, supermarkets, houses, and industries. It will be a suburban community or, if you like, a satellite community similar to several such successful communities that I have seen in England. Progress had been made on this project before the conference opened. We want to see more of the provinces undertaking this type of thing, and we want to see more of this activity in Ontario.
Would the minister permit a question?

At the end of my remarks. In the editorial aftermath of the conference it came through loud and clear that although the federal government had put forward these four progressive, important proposals, all of which were accepted by the provincial delegations, the federal government, according to editorial comment, did not seem to have the funds with which to implement them. What failed to emerge in even a single newspaper that I have read or in any news comment that I have heard was the fact that the government of Canada had already indicated that it was and is prepared to commit to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, for investment in 1968, funds substantially in excess of those budgeted for 1967 in these areas of greatest need, including those to which 1 have referred.

December 21, 1967
Housing
How much more?

I will deal with that in a minute or so. The second encouraging development arising out of the discussions last week was the agreement reached on a form of continuing study and assessment of the problems, to which reference was made this morning by the Prime Minister and other hon. members.
Criticism, Mr. Speaker, is always welcome if it is criticism of the right kind, and I will gladly accept some criticism here. Possibly it is deserved, probably it is deserved in some respects, but when people with a relatively superficial knowledge of all the factors that come into play in the current housing situation pose as experts, just like people who make a one week visit to Europe or Japan and return as experts on those countries-
Or the north.

-or the north, then I think we who have the responsibility should take issue with their superficial criticism. Many writers suggest in a superficial vein that the government has not provided effective leadership, or the leadership demanded by the circumstances. I would like to dispell that myth once and for all.
That will be a good effort.

And you will get it. This year housing starts throughout Canada will reach about 160,000, some 26,000 units above last year's total, the fourth largest number of unit starts in any year in Canada's history. The largest was in 1965, the second largest in 1964 and the third largest in 1958.
But that figure of 160,000 for 1967 starts does not include new housing accommodation that takes a form other than self-contained dwelling units. For example, much has been done to provide needed housing in the form of hostel accommodation in our large cities. Approval has been given in this year, 1967, to the provision of hostel accommodation for approximately 10,000 elderly people and students. Taking these into consideration, 1967 has been a record year for starts in housing accommodation, and this in spite of the fact that we had relatively few starts in the first quarter of the year. It has been achieved virtually in a period of nine months.
Having said that, Mr. Speaker, I would be less than candid if I failed to express disappointment about some of the things that happened, or rather failed to happen at the

recent housing conference. There was provision on the agenda for the discussion of a large number of urban problems that fall mainly within provincial jurisdiction. Some of these problems-pollution, urban traffic congestion, suburban resistance to low cost residential development, urban land costs, and the fragmentation of urban government planning-were on the agenda for discussion. One or two of them were discussed, but not in great depth.
I myself drew attention to these problems, as did several of my cabinet colleagues. I did so on at least two occasions, but to say the least it seemed to some of us that at least some of the heads of provincial delegations were not too anxious to discuss these sensitive matters. They seemed to feel that the federal government should not take anything but an academic interest in these questions.
One might conclude from some provincial comment made at the conference that these problems are well in hand, but I can assure hon. members, having lived with these problems for a number of years, that they are far from being well in hand. To give one instance, in the province of Ontario in certain circumstances you have to go through 42 different agencies in order to get permits to proceed with building of housing. It may well have seemed silly to one provincial premier to have a conference about questions where so much of the responsibility lies heavily on the provincial governments, but in my opinion certainly not nearly as silly as refusing to take advantage of the opportunity to discuss what could be done to bring down land costs, which is the largest single factor in housing in this country, particularly in our metropolitan areas. They did not try to come to grips with that problem, e (12:30 p.m.)
Housing is not just the problem of land assembly, because some encouraging progress is being made in some of the provinces in this field. More important than that is the problem in respect of the taxation structure and procedures. Surely the provinces should come to grips with the type of problem which was developed by reason of the fact that at the end of the war, or five or ten years following the war, entrepreneurs or land developers picked up lots for $1,000 to $1,200 and are now selling them for $10,000, $12,000 or $15,000 without any tax being involved. The representatives of the provinces should not
December 21, 1967

have been afraid to state their position openly in this regard before the television cameras here in Ottawa.
Believe me, there are many difficult, complex and massive problems which confront us with regard to the growth of our cities. If there is a reluctance on the part of some of the provinces to go beyond the exercise of their primary constitutional jurisdiction and reluctance to discuss the plans they have for exercising their prerogatives, then something is wrong and this is where the conference failed. If it failed it was because it was a federal-provincial conference and at such a conference one must expect contributions at both the federal and provincial level.

They did not get any
from you.

They may not have, in your opinion, but I must say, however, that we did put forward a few good views which they accepted. To put it in its simplest terms, while 1967 may not have been as big a year as all of us who have given serious thought to this problem would have liked to see it still was a big year in respect of housing in Canada. The significance of the government's leadership or, if I may put it another way, government action is manifest not only in the total volume of housing production for the year but in the fact that the proportion of accommodation for low income families and elderly citizens is considerably higher than ever before.
Hear, hear.

Indeed, housing for those whose needs are the most urgent has become such an important part of our total housing program that there is now available to these families a record number of dwellings. This has become more and more important. In my opinion there is nothing more important than the provision of homes for those who face difficulty in building their own homes and those who cannot relate a home of their own to their limited incomes.
Undoubtedly the most acute problems associated with rapid urbanization in Canada are being experienced in the province of Ontario. In that province, dwelling starts in Toronto in 1967 will set a new record over any other year. Perhaps we should do more, but do not say that we are not making any progress when we have moved from the low level of 1966 to a record level in 1967. About 50 per cent of these starts in Toronto were
Housing
financed under the National Housing Act. Close to 10 per cent represent accommodation for low income families, elderly citizens and students. In metropolitan Toronto alone more housing units will be started this year than the 32,000 produced in the record year of 1965 to which reference has been made.
While filling the leading position as the source of N.H.A. mortgage financing for accommodation produced on the market, the federal government has also been called upon throughout 1967 to increase sums for more specialized forms of housing such as public housing, housing for the elderly and housing for students. I should like to make clear that not only has there been no curtailment but also there has been no refusal of applications for funds for use in this way. We have every confidence that there will be an increase in 1968 of approximately 50 per cent in allocations of this nature. Listen to these figures. Ten years ago parliament voted some $35 million a year for public housing. When it became my responsibility to answer for Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in this house its total annual budget was $350 million. Only a niggardly portion of this was used for public housing, because the initiative in these fields rests at the municipal and provincial levels. There has been, however, a remarkable change as a result of the legislation passed by parliament in 1964, which I had the honour to introduce.
In the area of public housing alone in the year 1967 approximately 9,000 units will have been authorized. This is more than double the number in the year 1966. I would have liked to see twice that number, but we are making encouraging progress in that direction. What has been done in the year
1967	represents in one year one third of the total number of public housing starts provided in the whole of Canada in the last 20 years. I believe that is a record for which I do not have to apologize.
Hear, hear.

Public housing for low income families, for the elderly and for students is now a very significant part of Canada's annual building program and, as has been said by the Prime Minister, can be expected to have an even greater impact in
1968	and in the years ahead.
I should now like to review the prospects for the coming year in terms of anticipated federal financial commitments for housing programs which will continue under current

December 21, 1967
Housing
provisions of the National Housing Act. As I have already said more than once, we expect that the freeing of the interest rate on insured home-owner and rental loans will provide necessary flexibility and result in greatly increased participation by approved lenders. Having in mind the comment made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Patterson) this morning, I should like to put this on the record. He said hopes had been expressed that there would be improvement in the number of loans under the N.H.A. I am glad to assure the house that in- a period of just under 90 days there has not just been a hope of this happening but rather in October and November by means of N.H.A. loans four times as many dwellings have been started than in the corresponding period of last year-four times as many.
At the conference last week the Prime Minister stated that we were following this situation and that if we did not obtain satisfactory results we might have to take other action. There is not the slightest doubt that we are now getting these results. Anyone who believes in free or private enterprise will realize that if they can obtain a certain interest rate from a company which wants to build a factory, a pipe line, an office building or a warehouse, they are not likely to put this money into housing if the interest rate in respect of housing is one per cent or half a per cent lower. I think we did what was the realistic thing to do. We did not fix the interest rate at 8-J per cent. We did what parliament authorized and said that approved lending institutions-and they have to be approved before they can obtain the benefits of the act-could make loans at an interest rate up to that ceiling. 1 am happy to say that some of the lending institutions, including insurance companies and at least one of the larger banks, are lending money at an interest rate substantially below the ceiling, one half of one per cent below.
[DOT] (12:40 p.m.)
This flexibility is bringing more money into the field of housing and accounts in part at least for the fact that the last nine months of 1967 we have had a record period for housing starts in Canada. In addition, the government is making more money available in the areas of greatest need, for public housing and projects of that kind. Not only the proportion but the level of commitments in these areas of greatest public need will increase. At the same time-I want to make this clear for the record at this time-that

not only will there be more funds available for the areas of greatest social need but a substantial sum has been earmarked for 1968 for those who wish to build their own homes and may not be able to arrange financing through direct loans.
We have cut back on speculative builders' loans, those who build for profit. Let them go to the private lending institutions to borrow money and make their profit in the usual way. There is nothing wrong with that in a country like Canada. There has been and will be in the rural parts of Canada greater difficulty in getting loans from the traditional lending institutions because they do not have offices and inspectors there, so C.M.H.C. will have funds available for direct loans to people who want to build their own homes.
Reference was made this morning, and I referred to this matter during the conference, to the revival of the limited dividend program to provide rental housing for moderate income families. Provision is being made for a renewed, a wider, program of this type. This program, as I am sure most hon. members know though others may not, was very successful in the first few years of its operation. Today, however, if you have an income of more than $5,400 in some areas-I think it is $5,500 in one-you are not eligible to acquire a house under the limited dividend program. The program is tied in with one's income. The private speculator puts up a portion of the money and C.M.H.C. is prepared to finance the balance, but the return to the private speculator is limited to 5 per cent. This is not very realistic when you realize that in Ontario the rate on government loans is about 7J per cent, in Quebec it is about 7J per cent and in my own native province of New Brunswick it is 7J per cent. The federal government is paying about 6 per cent. Therefore a 5 per cent interest rate is realistic in respect of limited dividend housing.
We propose to make changes by way of regulation or legislation, if necessary, to put the limited dividend program back into effect. C.M.H.C. is now ready to receive applications from entrepreneurs, land developers, builders or anyone else. This money will be available on attractive terms that are being widely announced throughout the country, which I believe will put this program back on its feet. It may take time to get limited dividend projects under way on the scale we would like, because it must be
December 21, 1967

remembered that the program has been inactive for years and it will take a little time to revive it.
One of the major areas of investment of federal funds in 1968 will be loans to provinces and municipalities for public housing projects, land assembly for housing, sewage treatment plants, and this type of project. There was a slight disagreement at the housing conference between the prime minister of Quebec and myself with regard to amending the legislation, but when I explained to him that the federal government was quite prepared to recommend to parliament that funds be made available for the acquisition of land for housing, provided it would not be held by the province for 50 years and would not become the property of the province, with the taxpayers of Canada paying the shot and the asset being turned over to the province, the disagreement was resolved. We will make loans for these projects on a short term basis of 10 or 15 years at low rates. This money will be available to provinces who wish to acquire land for housing. There would be no profit in it. the reason; it is as simple as that. If we are to make provision for the money needed for public housing, student housing, land assembly and urban renewal in areas where urban renewal is vital, we cannot put money into speculative building, much as I might like to.
Reference was made, again by the hon. member for Fraser Valley for whom I have very high regard, to the winter building bonus of $500 but there is one thing that the hon. member overlooked. He referred to the $500 winter house building bonus that was instituted in 1963. This bonus was paid on each unit built during the winter months and was carried on through the winters from 1963, 1964, and 1965, dropped last year.
I would like to make this clear so there can be no dispute about it. The $500 bonus would have been largely meaningless had it not been for the almost unlimited funds that were made available to speculative builders who were building for profit. They were building on speculation and the federal government was providing the funds for that purpose. If it is a choice between providing funds for that purpose or for areas of greater need, we certainly will go to the areas of greater need.
Our policy in this respect seems to be working. There is a reasonable level of interest rates. If with our concentration of effort on public housing and allied problems we do not obtain the results we expect, I am not prepared to say that we will not take another look at the speculative lending program, but our present program does not contemplate any speculative lending for 1968.

maintopic: MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT DESCENDANTS OF FATHERS OF CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. As this is the last scheduled day on which this parliament will be sitting in the one hundredth year of confederation, I should like to draw the attention of the house to the fact that there are two men sitting in the House of Commons who are direct descendants of the fathers of confederation. I believe that December 21 is observed as the anniversary of the death of one of these gentlemen, namely Hon. Edward Whelan, of whom Eugene Whelan, the hon. member for Essex South, is a direct descendant. May I also say that the hon. member for Lotbiniere, Mr. Auguste Choquette, is a direct descendant of Sir Pascal Tache who at one time was the prime minister of Canada and who was the hon. member's great-great-grandfather. The French have a knack for keeping track of their family connections and can trace back their forbears for many generations. There is no question that the hon. member for Lotbiniere is a direct descendant of Sir Pascal Tache.
The Irish were more of a wandering type, but it can be proved that the hon. member for Essex South is a direct descendant of Hon. Edward Whelan who represented Prince Edward Island at the second Quebec conference and who also attended the Charlottetown conference. Sir Pascal Tache presided over the first Quebec conference but unfortunately passed away before the other two meetings were held. Hon. Edward Whelan was a printer, a man after my own heart, and to prove that there is a direct connection between him and the hon. member for Essex South may I quote a few words from an editorial in the Saint John, New Brunswick Globe of December 21, 1867. Speaking of the Hon. Edward Whelan, this is what it said:
Mr. Whelan enlisted with ardour on the side of the people, and soon drew down upon himself the stern opposition of the old and powerful family compact which ruled the island.

December 21, 1967
Royal Assent
May I say that this is in keeping with the cool breezes now blowing in this direction from the other place. It continues:
His long public career has been characterized by a firm and eloquent advocacy of measures calculated to improve and elevate the people. He was a man of large sympathies, of quick and generous nature, of ready wit, and with an eye always to the humorous side of a question. An extensive and varied reader, a man of excellent literary and of considerable natural eloquence, he was a flowing and imaginative speaker.

On clause 2-Broadcasting policy for Canada.

Mr. Chairman, when the house adjourned yesterday I had just started to make a few remarks about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and this proposed legislation, Bill No. C-163. The bill is divided readily into three parts. We are now discussing clause 2 of part I which in essence sets out the objects of a broadcasting policy that the government hopes to project across Canada.
I came to Ottawa ten years ago, Mr. Chairman. If I were asked to look back and to single out a subject that has continually caused more concern to members of parliament and to this and the previous government I would have to say it was the C.B.C. and its administration and management. During those ten years the broadcasting committee has held meetings and studied broadcasting legislation from time to time. We have had the C.B.C. management on the mat, so to speak, time and time again. The point I am trying to make is that there seems to be no way in which the government and members of parliament can control this communications system and at the same time keep out of the field. And one really has to have control over this mammoth giant which continues to spend the taxpayers' money at an amazing rate. The taxpayers are not completely happy with the way the corporation is run in that no one seems to be able to control it, and no one in the corporation seems to take responsibility for some of the things it does.
The bill before the committee, seeks to set up a Canadian radio-television council, which will be a completely independent body. In other words, the management and operations of this mammoth giant will be removed that much farther from the people who pay for its operations and from their representatives. Members of parliament and the people generally will have little or no influence over the
December 21, 1967

controlling of the C.B.C. or over the projection of a Canadian content and a Canadian culture in its programs.
According to the objects outlined in the clause, it appears that the council will have to go further and contribute to the unity of Canada and assist Canadians in developing a national identity. In other words, it seems that the council is going to be a very powerful board which, if it takes its work seriously, will have the ability to brainwash Canadians all across Canada in such a way as to shape our unity and identity. I question whether this is right, Mr. Chairman. One hon. member speaking in the debate yesterday likened the C.B.C. as a means of communication to something not very different from a newspaper. Certainly the corporation is not too different from a newspaper. A government should not become involved in the publication of a daily or weekly newspaper, so why should it become involved in a now established television network or even, for that matter, a radio network?
In 1932 when the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was first set up it was the duty of the government to foster the development of a broadcasting network for Canada. We now have one network established with perhaps more on the way, and I suggest that at this point government should attempt to phase itself out of the operations of the C.B.C. Certainly, parliament should phase itself out of controlling the C.B.C. or we should put the corporation up for sale and let someone else run it. Some body similar to the Board of Broadcast Governors must impose regulations to control broadcasting.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The Minister of Finance has said that we are in a difficult financial position and that certain cuts must be made here and there. Not long ago the Prime Minister said that all the money which might have been available for housing had been completely absorbed by other expenditures. The Minister of National Revenue has cut agricultural payments to farmers because there is a shortage of money. Yet under this bill another large governing council is to be set up. In her opening remarks when introducing the bill the minister said that this council would need to employ more civil servants than any similar body has ever employed before. Instead of cutting down on the number of new employees the minister, through this bill, is seeking to increase their number.

Canadians are asking that government be simplified and that costs of government be reduced. Statistics show that one of every eight Canadians works for government at some level. In effect, our society has become so complicated that out of every eight people one controls the other seven. We should attempt to simplify our society and cut government expenditures instead of increasing them. The Minister of National Revenue said that the government will make a concerted effort to limit the growth of the civil service. Yet the Secretary of State under this bill is seeking to employ an ever-increasing number of civil servants.
Parliament must control this giant, the C.B.C. The minister quite obviously has found it almost impossible to control the giant. I sat on the broadcasting committees some years ago and we studied the question of broadcasting. What tests is one to apply to taste? Who can judge what is in good taste and what is not? If this is a free society, as I hope it is, then economics must be the judge. As the hon. member for Kindersley said yesterday, surely no one would buy a film like "Waiting For Caroline", broadcast it across Canada and expect to make money on it. The corporation spent $319,000 making that film, and the Minister of Finance has increased taxes by 5 per cent. It has not been set up yet.

I know that, but I do not think that we should compete with Hollywood. We should not use taxpayers' dollars for a risky enterprise like the film business. Nor should we compete with Hollywood. Certainly the government must enact broadcasting legislation, but I think that the government should get out of broadcasting. If the C.B.C. is a going concern we should put it up for sale. Let someone buy this Canadian corporation about which everyone is talking. I do not care who buys it. I do care about the taxpayers and the way their money is spent. The government should not be involved in a risky, gambling type of enterprise such as the film business. As I said, we should not compete with Hollywood and the government should not attempt to brainwash the public.
The purpose of this legislation, we are told, is to safeguard, enrich and strengthen Canada. How can you safeguard, enrich and strengthen Canada without brainwashing people? It cannot be done otherwise. We are also told that those with conflicting views will be allowed to express those views on C.B.C. networks. Sometimes, I have the impression that only one side of a picture has been presented on certain programs. The other side has been ignored. Both sides of an argument ought to be fairly presented.
The bill is to contribute to the development of national unity. How can any piece of legislation or any council that is set up contribute to the development of national unity? How is that possible without somebody trying to brainwash the people? That just does not make sense. we should not be in the broadcasting business because it is risky and requires a great deal of capital.

The setting up of a council will remove the corporation even farther from parliamentary control. The cry in parliament for many years has been that nobody has any control over the corporation. The bill provides every escape route feasible for C.B.C. management as a way out should any complaints reach them. So we are giving the corporation in effect a blank cheque covering anything they may wish to disseminate.
This giant has grown so big that instead of trying to limit its size we are washing our hands of it and handing it over to someone else to run. In my opinion we are going about handling this mammoth giant, which each year is gobbling up more money and creating disharmony rather than unity in Canada, in the wrong way. In rising this afternoon to speak on this proposed broadcasting bill I can tell you, Mr. Chairman and members of the House of Commons, that I do so with a heavy heart. I consider myself a Liberal. I am one of the privileged men of this country in that I was able to enjoy a close association with the late Joseph E. Dickinson, publisher and editor of the Toronto Star to the date of his death in 1948, and if there is anyone in this house who wishes to question the Liberal antecedents of the Toronto Star I am here to answer him.
It is true that the Toronto Star took a stand with regard to Liberal policy in 1917 and that the Star proved to be right, even if it did support a unionist government. I have taken part in every election campaign provincially since 1919 when I scruti-neered for the late George A. Gillespie, Liberal candidate for re-election in Peterborough that year. I have here in my hand a XEROX copy of a judgment handed down by the supreme court of British Columbia in a celebrated case regarding the Public Utilities Commission of British Columbia and Victoria Cable-vision et al. This decision was rendered by the supreme court of British Columbia. The decision rendered there and the opinions of the various justices are worthy of study. Canadian Policy on Broadcasting provision of alternative television service in that general region. Mr. Chairman, ladies and gentlemen, this is quite interesting. Three applications by John Albulet of Ottawa for C.A.T.V. systems in Prescott, Ganaboque and Napanee were turned down on the ground that they would inhibit the provision of alternative television service in that general region. I made inquiries and found that the people in Gananoque and Napanee pick up the Kingston station which is privately owned.
I do not know how familiar hon. members are with the operation of C.A.T.V. installations, but the point one must bear in mind is that if you are the owner of a television station and have a licence from the government you possess a very valuable franchise. The more viewers you have, the higher the advertising rates you can charge the people who may wish to make use of your television station. But if any influence comes into play which reduces the size of your audience, the advertisers will not willingly pay any rate which you as the owner of the station wish to charge. They will argue with you; they will show you that your audience of viewers is not as big as you claim it is, particularly if there are C.A.T.V. installations in the neighbourhood. I say to you quite frankly, honestly and without fear of contradiction that the television station owners do not want the people in their immediate territory looking at the programs of other stations because when they look at other stations' programs they reduce the size of the audience the local T.V. station operator is seeking to sell to advertisers.
I have mentioned in the house before today the interesting set-up at the lakehead at Port Arthur and Fort William where they have a T.V. station. I believe there are about 24,000 or 25,000 homes at the lakehead and there is one television station. The people at the lakehead are so pleased at the fact that they can look only at the one station that more than half of them, over 13,000 subscribers in Port Arthur, pay $5 a month so they will not have to look only at the Port Arthur station and can have their choice of Duluth-Superior or Marquette in Michigan. When over 13,000 families are willing to pay approximately $5 a month for C.A.T.V. service because there is only one station in the area, what better commentary do you need in respect of whether or not the Canadian station is meeting the desires and wishes of the people of Canada?

The C.A.T.V. applicant was denied licences for Gananoque and Napanee. Mr. Chairman, I had this information from the Secretary of State (Miss LaMarsh) about those two private television stations in Quebec city, namely, CFCM-TV on channel 4 and CKMI-TV on channel 5, both of which are owned by Television de Quebec (Canada) Limitee, and my remarks are in connection with clause 2(b), which states that:

The previous law similarly provided that majority ownership of radio and television stations in Canada be held by Canadians. Now, majority ownership of the two Quebec city stations I have referred to is not held by Canadian residents; this is why they operate under an order in council dating from 1965; in fact, although majority ownership of those stations is held by foreign interests, they operate in Canada nevertheless, under an order in council which protects their majority shareholders and empowers them to do so.
The minister sent me the list of the directors, where interesting things are to be found concerning what is happening in the field of television in Quebec.
The president of the Quebec city TV station, Television-Quebec-Canada Ltee, which controls and owns both Quebec stations, is Mr. Gaston Pratte, president and director, who holds one common share on the 10,000 existing shares. Boldstad. I do not know where he comes from, no address is mentioned, but he is also holder of one single share, as treasurer and director. Fitzgibbons-who, I believe, is the son of the vice-president and also comes

from Toronto. The general manager, however, Mr. Jean A. Pouliot, holds 500 shares. This means that there are seven who only have one share each and one who has 500 of the 10,000 shares.

The wording of the act is as follows:
It is hereby declared-
I am referring to clause 2 (b),
-that the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled-[DOT]

I see that the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) is now in the house. I ask the minister to believe that there are many people in the province of Quebec who ask nothing better than to buy shares in one of the Quebec television stations, since they are probably among the stations which make the most money in Canada. Canadian Policy on Broadcasting of Quebec would like to invest money in this concern.

-the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians-

Mr. Chairman, during the committee discussion, I raised the matter, and the minister told me then that she did

The great problem of Canadian solidarity is based precisely on the existence of a sound barrier. In some regions of Canada, French consonances seem as strange as Hebrew or Arab consonances and this gives rise to frustrations and often to deplorable acts of extremism. It would be quite interesting, especially for the younger generation of English speaking Canadians who are unusually open-minded, to recognize more and more that the French fact is valuable for Canada and helps us precisely to distinguish ourseves from Americans and to check growing Americanism.
In school, youngsters are given some notions and rudiments of French and after leaving school, they have no opportunity to improve their knowledge. That is the reason why I should like, with the same emphasis, ask the hon. minister to act promptly, in order to establish everywhere, in Canada, relay stations of the French network, which would cost very little.

I note that clause 2(c) of Bill C-163 reads:
(c) all persons licensed to carry on broadcasting undertakings have a responsibility for the public effects of the programs they broadcast but the right to freedom of expression, subject only to generally applicable statutes and regulations, is unquestioned;
I also note that clause 39(1), which we shall be discussing later, reads:
The corporation is established for the purpose of providing the national broadcasting service contemplated by section 2 of this act,-
And so on. Here the bill stipulates clearly that clause 2 applies not only to all licensed broadcasters but to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as well.
Here we are dealing with a matter of accountability: Who shall be held accountable for the programs which come out of the television tube or the radio receiver? The bill is quite clear-as it needs to be, and it is vital that no one misunderstands its meaning-that persons who are licensed, and the management of the C.B.C., are to be held accountable. I raise this point because of my experiences during the past two years on the broadcasting committee as well as a result of my own researches.
Those of us on the broadcasting committee last year saw a bitter war raging within the C.B.C. between the producers of "This Hour has Seven Days" and some of their immediate superiors, and the management of the corporation. A small but determined group of producers made a bare faced attempt to destroy the corporation's top management, because top management had had the temerity to suggest that, in the face of public demand and demands made in this house to end serious breaches of good taste and the flagrant slanting of programs, a slanting which was against the best interests of the country, the program be toned down.
Not content with trying to unseat those in authority, these people at public expense instituted a telephone campaign from a hotel room opposite the C.B.C. offices in Toronto, to try to stir up protests on their behalf. One may read the details in the committee's reports. Mr. LaPierre, Mr. Watson and Mr. Canadian Policy on Broadcasting Leiterman also engaged in speaking engagements and in radio and television performances to build up their campaign against their so-called tormentors in C.B.C. management. Last year, following this extraordinary performance, I wrote in Canada Month:
Only forty people worked on the staff of '7 Days' -8,500 are employed at C.B.C. Yet the producers and performers of this relatively small group were able to resist and test the strength of the entire C.B.C. management while attempting to force the Canadian government and parliament to act on its behalf. Their strength was multiplied dangerously through the astonishing power of T.V. and by a carefully manipulated campaign in the press and on Parliament Hill. Seldom have Canadians seen such an occurrence that so occupied the country's attention and so scarred the image of the massive C.B.C. operation.
Unfortunately, press, radio and television supported the producers at first, but management of C.B.C. was given its right to manage and Mr. Leiterman, Mr. Watson and Mr. LaPierre left for politics and other fields. I note that Maclean's magazine pictured Laurier LaPierre on a recent cover as Canada's first socialist prime minister. May I ask this question: Did Mr. LaPierre's left wing politics start immediately after he left the C.B.C. or were Canadians who watched his program treated to a barrage of his thinking and ideas and the special ideas that his friends had? That program was supposed to be an objective but startling look at the world today. I think you know the answer, and I shall provide some specific evidence when we deal with the clauses of the bill.

Grievances could thus be dealt with promptly and equitably, thereby preventing the dispute from becoming a matter of public controversy.

We must make certain that this bill gives the new management of the C.B.C. a clear mandate to enforce a policy which is also clearly stated in the bill, and that the C.B.C. management, not the producers, are accountable and responsible for what comes out of the T.V. tube or over the air waves. This does not mean, nor should it mean, a continuing war between both sides of broadcasting, but what it does mean is that when management says "do" or "don't", producers "do" or "don't"-or leave the corporation. Of course producers and artists are sensitive people and must be worked with carefully so that their talents are brought to bear on suitable subject matter. But let me remind the producers that the listening audiences of Canada are also sensitive people, and they elect members to parliament to see that in certain respects their wishes are carried out.
Section 2 of the Broadcasting Act states in paragraph (i) that the national broadcasting service should be among other things, a balanced service of information. It is essential that members of this house and the country at large should understand how badly unbalanced a performance we have been given in certain areas of broadcasting. Let me say right away, however, that there has been a noticeable improvement since this fuss was made in parliament. But not enough. The nature of the problems Canada faces in its broadcasting system and the serious nature of these issues can only be evaluated when we understand the power of broadcasting itself.
This power of broadcasting was thus ably described by the British broadcasting committee of 1949 in a report to the British parliament:
Broadcasting is the most persuasive, and therefore one of the most powerful agents for influencing men's thoughts and action, for giving them a picture, true or false, of their fellows of the world in which they live, for appealing to their intellect, their emotions and their appetites, for filling their minds with beauty or ugliness, ideas or idleness, laughter or care, love or hate.

Some of these problems are glaringly evident. Some time ago when Tom Gould resigned from the C.B.C. over the breach of good faith in using a story taken from a closed meeting at which the former leader of the opposition spoke, Dennis Braithwaite wrote in the Globe and Mail:

I have been doing a little study on this matter and I think the writer has put his finger on the point-lack of professionalism in the journalistic area. And where does most of the trouble lie? It lies with our old friends in the public affairs field who try to usurp the news field and give Canadians twisted versions of the facts, or, as the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister stated earlier in this debate, try to influence us through the process of distortion by omission. Two years ago we were saturated by C.B.C. public affairs programs, with a vast documentary done by Patrick Watson and his allies on the wondrous advances being made by Red China. I have not noticed the rush of these same producers to give us another vast documentary on the tragic terrorism of the Red Guard which has engulfed China. Why have they not been interviewing the thousands of refugees who have fled the terror of that upside down world into Hong Kong, Formosa and elsewhere? Why have they not sent a camera crew up to the Northern borders of India where almost every week the Chinese army conducts raids into India? And, even more important, why have we not had from Patrick Watson and his friends a full documentary on the rape of Tibet- which still goes on-and which they conveniently left out of their China documentary? Tens of thousands of Tibetans have escaped, and do so daily-and now live next door to starvation in northern India.
Canadians need to know the full truth from the C.B.C. To add further fuel to the fire, let us examine how accurate a picture we are getting on the serious racial problem in the United States. We have been deluged with one-sided views of the American racial

DEBATES	December 21, 1967
issue on the C.B.C. The much advertised one-hour presentation a few weeks ago on American police preparation for riot control was a clear endeavour to create an anti-U.S. atmosphere. Then again, a veritable orgy of hate came over our T.V. screens when on September 24th this year the program "The Way It Is" interviewed extremist negroes.
Why do we never see the other side of the story-the very extensive improvements which have been made in a number of areas in race relations across the border? This year for example, on American television on November 15 came an excellent presentation of a successful desegregation experiment at the elementary school level in Evanston, Illinois. The vast majority of schools in the United States have been integrated. But this great success story is never told to Canadians. Why have we not been told that in western Europe only 8 per cent of all its youth enter university, but 15 per cent of all United States negro youths enter university. And there are many more statistics of this kind. You have heard Rap Brown, Stokely Carmichael and other extremist negro leaders interviewed over C.B.C. Why have we not heard the moderate majority leaders over C.B.C.?
And last but not least, I have a statement by Rev. Garth Hunt, dated Ottawa, December 17, 1967. Rev. Garth Hunt is a Canadian missionary, who has been in South Viet Nam for ten years and was back in Canada for five months prior to his return to South Viet Nam. He knows the country intimately, facilitated by his excellent working knowledge of the Vietnamese language. This devoted Canadian missionary has been travelling across the continent on a speaking engagement since his return, and was interviewed numerous times by commentators on T.V. and radio in different Canadian cities regarding his experience in Viet Nam. I met him in Viet Nam last summer. He has given me this statement:
The great bulk of the news and Information about Viet Nam which I have heard and seen particularly on Canadian radio and T.V. programs since returning to this country, closely approximates the propaganda emanating from North Viet Nam. It is not only misleading, but a great deal of the time is in direct contradiction with the realities I saw and experienced myself during my ten years in South Viet Nam and especially during the past year when I covered more than 10,000 miles of that country examining the situation at close hand.
Furthermore, many of the news commentators with whom I have appeared on my Canadian trip have, following the broadcast when I have
December 21, 1967

presented the facts from Viet Nam, asked this question-"Why are we not getting this other side of the story from C.B.C. news commentators and commentators"?-I can only come to this conclusion that Canadians are being misled by the news gathering and communications media in only getting one side of the story.
This act must be so clear in its mandate to the management of C.B.C. and the private stations that never again will Canadians be plagued with barefaced distortions and serious omissions over the air waves. If we are to play our part in shaping a workable world, we can only do so if we are given factual, balanced and fair presentations of news, information and viewpoints. Unbalanced presentations also lead to pressures on government that can be dangerous to the democratic system. Freedom is a precious jewel and it is our job to preserve it. This act is an important weapon in the continuing battle.
May I ask the hon. member a question? To his knowledge has this Mr. Garth Hunt been asked to appear on the C.B.C. to present the other side of the story?

I can find that out.
